claim: Life expectancy has risen sharply in the last 50 years.
source: Life expectancy has risen sharply in the last 50 years.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the data and analyses presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: The Michaelis-Menten enzyme kinetics model can be applied to demonstrate a mathematical relationship of income to childhood (aged 0-5 years) and adult (aged 15-60 years) survival.
source: We applied the classic Michaelis–Menten enzyme kinetics to demonstrate a novel mathematical relationship of income to childhood (aged 0–5 years) and adult (aged 15–60 years) survival.
evidence: The manuscript presents the application of the MM model to mortality data for 180 countries from 1970 to 2007.

claim: Maximum child and adult survival rose by about 1% per year.
source: Maximum child and adult survival rose by about 1% per year.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data in Table 3 and Figure 3A showing increases in maximum survival rates.

claim: Critical incomes fell by half for children from 1970 to 2007.
source: Critical incomes fell by half for children
evidence: Table 3 shows child critical income declining from $0.58 in 1970 to $0.24 in 2005, and the text states it fell by over half.

claim: Critical incomes doubled for men from 1970 to 2007.
source: Critical incomes fell by half for children, but doubled for men.
evidence: Table 3 shows male critical income rising from $0.54 in 1970 to $1.14 in 2005, more than doubling.

claim: HIV infection and smoking account for some, but not all, of the rising critical incomes for adult survival.
source: HIV infection and smoking account for some, but not all, of the rising critical incomes for adult survival.
evidence: Figure 5 and Table 4 show that adjusting for HIV and smoking reduces critical income but does not fully explain the increase.

claim: Global life expectancy rose by about 90 days per year in the 20th century, with much of that increase driven by substantial declines in childhood mortality.
source: In the 20th century, global life expectancy rose by about 90 days per year, with much of that increase driven by substantial declines in childhood mortality (Oeppen, 2002; Vallin and Meslé, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oeppen (2002) and Vallin and Meslé (2009).

claim: In most low-income countries, death in middle age is increasing in relative importance as other causes decrease and the effects of smoking increase.
source: In most low-income countries, death in middle age is increasing in relative importance as other causes decrease and the effects of smoking increase (Jha, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jha (2009).

claim: Most adult deaths are due to noncommunicable diseases, such as vascular, respiratory, or neoplastic diseases, with a significant minority due to HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis.
source: Most adult deaths are due to noncommunicable diseases, such as vascular, respiratory, or neoplastic diseases, with a significant minority due to HIV/AIDS, malaria, and tuberculosis (Beaglehole et al., 2011b).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Beaglehole et al. (2011b).

claim: Preston (1975) established a cross-sectional relationship between mean national life expectancy and national income per capita.
source: In a classic paper, Preston (1975) offered an elegant analysis to establish a cross-sectional relationship between mean national life expectancy and national income per capita.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Preston (1975).

claim: The Preston curve shows a positive relationship between national income levels and life expectancy in poorer countries but with smaller marginal returns at higher incomes.
source: The 'Preston curve' shows a positive relationship between national income levels and life expectancy in poorer countries but with smaller marginal returns at higher incomes.
evidence: This is a description of the Preston curve, supported by Figure 1A and the citation to Preston (1975).

claim: Preston noted an upward rise in the curve for three decades over the 20th century, leading to higher life expectancies for any given national income level over time.
source: Preston noted an upward rise in the curve for three decades over the 20th century, leading to higher life expectancies for any given national income (defined as GDP per capita) level over time (Figure 1A is a reproduced graph of the Preston curve for the years 1960 and 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by reference to Figure 1A and the citation to Preston (1975).

claim: The upward rise in the Preston curve has been attributed to the adoption of low-cost health technologies for child survival, such as immunization and oral rehydration.
source: This upward rise has been attributed to the adoption of low-cost health technologies for child survival (Mathers et al., 2008; United Nations, 2011), such as immunization and oral rehydration
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Mathers et al. (2008) and United Nations (2011).

claim: The upward rise in the Preston curve has been attributed to improvements in nutrition.
source: This upward rise has been attributed to the adoption of low-cost health technologies for child survival (Mathers et al., 2008; United Nations, 2011), such as immunization and oral rehydration, and to improvements in nutrition (Fogel, 1997)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Fogel (1997).

claim: The upward rise in the Preston curve has been attributed to improvements in sanitation.
source: This upward rise has been attributed to the adoption of low-cost health technologies for child survival (Mathers et al., 2008; United Nations, 2011), such as immunization and oral rehydration, and to improvements in nutrition (Fogel, 1997), sanitation (Cutler and Miller, 2004)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cutler and Miller (2004).

claim: The upward rise in the Preston curve has been attributed to primary education for women.
source: This upward rise has been attributed to the adoption of low-cost health technologies for child survival (Mathers et al., 2008; United Nations, 2011), such as immunization and oral rehydration, and to improvements in nutrition (Fogel, 1997), sanitation (Cutler and Miller, 2004), primary education for women (Caldwell, 1979; Cutler et al., 2006)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Caldwell (1979) and Cutler et al. (2006).

claim: Some countries such as Costa Rica, Cuba, and Sri Lanka all achieve life expectancy levels greater than expected by their income.
source: Indeed, some countries such as Costa Rica, Cuba, and Sri Lanka all achieve life expectancy levels greater than expected by their income (Caldwell, 1986).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Caldwell (1986).

claim: Life expectancy has continued to increase globally.
source: Life expectancy has continued to increase globally
evidence: This is a general statement supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There is a belief that less daily income is required to achieve a certain life expectancy level.
source: Life expectancy has continued to increase globally, and this has led to the belief that less daily income is required to achieve a certain life expectancy level (Casabonne and Kenny, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Casabonne and Kenny (2012).

claim: The majority of gains in life expectancy for low- and middle-income countries have been achieved through reductions in child mortality while improvements in adult mortality have been restricted mostly to high-income countries.
source: In this article, we argue that the majority of gains in life expectancy for low- and middle-income countries have been achieved through reductions in child mortality while improvements in adult mortality have been restricted mostly to high-income countries.
evidence: This is a central argument of the manuscript, supported by the data in Tables 1 and 3 and Figures 3 and 4.

claim: Reductions in child mortality have reduced inequality between countries for child survival.
source: This has reduced inequality between countries for child survival
evidence: This is inferred from the declining critical income for children shown in Table 3 and Figure 3B.

claim: Improvements in adult mortality restricted to high-income countries have increased inequality for adult survival.
source: however, increased inequality for adult survival
evidence: This is inferred from the rising critical income for adults shown in Table 3 and Figure 3B.

claim: Critical income is analogous to the Michaelis constant (Km).
source: More specifically, we establish a new parameter 'critical income' (analogous to the Michaelis constant [Km])
evidence: This is stated explicitly in the introduction and explained in the methods section.

claim: The Michaelis-Menten mathematical model was initially developed to analyze enzyme kinetics.
source: The Michaelis–Menten mathematical model first described in 1913 (Michaelis and Menten, 1913) was initially developed to analyze enzyme kinetics.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Michaelis and Menten (1913).

claim: Enzymes are biomacromolecules that act as catalysts, agents that accelerate the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process.
source: Enzymes are biomacromolecules that act as catalysts, agents that accelerate the rate of a chemical reaction without being consumed in the process.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about enzymes.

claim: Km is the half saturation constant—substrate concentration at which ν = 0.5νmax.
source: Km is the half saturation constant—substrate concentration at which ν = 0.5νmax.
evidence: This is a standard definition in enzyme kinetics.

claim: A lower Km value indicates a more efficient catalyst.
source: Km is a function of the forward and reverse reaction rate constants, where a lower Km value indicates a more efficient catalyst
evidence: This is established knowledge in enzyme kinetics.

claim: GDP is treated as a substrate that is catalyzed to increase survival from technologies that income buys.
source: We treat income as a substrate that is catalyzed to increase survival (from technologies that income buys) for 180 countries from 1970 and 2007.
evidence: This is the conceptual framework of the manuscript, applying the MM model to income and survival.

claim: Infrastructure, vaccinations, and public health knowledge can be viewed as catalysts that are not consumed in entirety during the process.
source: Indeed, infrastructure (such as water sanitation and education systems), vaccinations (leading to long-term immunity), and public health knowledge can be viewed as catalysts that are not consumed in entirety during the process.
evidence: This is a conceptual argument made by the authors to justify the MM model application.

claim: Critical income is defined as the level of daily income associated with the achievement of 50% of the maximum life expectancy.
source: This construct is defined as the level of daily income associated with the achievement of 50% of the maximum life expectancy (i.e., GDP per capita at e0 = 0.5 × e0,max)
evidence: This is the definition provided by the authors for their new parameter.

claim: Maximum life expectancy is empiric, approximating the observed average life expectancy in high-income countries.
source: 'maximum life expectancy' is empiric, approximating the observed average life expectancy in high-income countries (Rodgers, 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to Rodgers (2002).

claim: Two times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 66.7% of the maximal life expectancy.
source: In particular, two, four, and nine times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 66.7%, 80%, and 90% of the maximal life expectancy, respectively.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the MM equation as applied by the authors.

claim: Four times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 80% of the maximal life expectancy.
source: In particular, two, four, and nine times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 66.7%, 80%, and 90% of the maximal life expectancy, respectively.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the MM equation as applied by the authors.

claim: Nine times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 90% of the maximal life expectancy.
source: In particular, two, four, and nine times the critical income yields the income required to achieve 66.7%, 80%, and 90% of the maximal life expectancy, respectively.
evidence: This is a mathematical property of the MM equation as applied by the authors.

claim: The asymptotic leveling of life expectancy at high income is analogous to the saturation of enzymatic sites at high substrate concentration.
source: The asymptotic leveling of life expectancy at high income seen in the Preston or MM curves is analogous to the saturation of enzymatic sites at high substrate concentration, thus, further increases in GDP leads to only marginal increases in life expectancy.
evidence: This is an analogy drawn by the authors to explain the MM model application.

claim: There was no significant difference in the coefficient of determination (R2) for the logistic, log-linear, and MM regressions from 1970 to 2007.
source: For the years 1970 to 2007, there was no significant difference in the coefficient of determination (R2) for the logistic (M = 0.666, SD = 0.064), log-linear (M = 0.645, SD = 0.073), and MM regressions (M = 0.622, SD = 0.083; F(2,26) = 0.807, p=0.458, not statistically significant)
evidence: This is a statistical result from the analysis comparing model fits.

claim: The MM model is statistically as valid as the Preston log-linear and logistic models.
source: indicating that the MM model is statistically as valid as the Preston log-linear and logistic models.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the statistical comparison of R2 values.

claim: The parameters of the logistic and log-linear models have less obvious explanatory value compared to the MM model.
source: Although the fits of the models were comparable, the parameters of the logistic and log-linear models have less obvious explanatory value.
evidence: This is an argument made by the authors based on the interpretation of model parameters.

claim: All inflection points for the logistic function were determined to be negative (from −$2.69 in 1970 to −$8.47 in 2007) and are impossible income values for any country.
source: For the logistic function, all inflection points were determined to be negative (from −$2.69 in 1970 to −$8.47 in 2007) and are impossible income values for any country.
evidence: This is a result from the logistic model analysis.

claim: The logistic function is overly complex and not necessary to model the data.
source: This suggests that the logistic function is overly complex and not necessary to model the data.
evidence: This is an inference drawn by the authors from the negative inflection points.

claim: For the log-linear function, the model parameters did not allow for a means to intuitively track lateral movements in the Preston curve.
source: For the log-linear function, the model parameters did not allow for a means to intuitively track lateral movements in the Preston curve.
evidence: This is an argument made by the authors about the limitations of the log-linear model.

claim: When using annual income (rather than daily income), the parameter 'a' in the log-linear model was not statistically significant for any year from 1970 to 2000.
source: In addition, when using annual income (rather than daily income), the parameter 'a' was not statistically significant for any year from 1970 to 2000.
evidence: This is a statistical result from the log-linear model analysis.

claim: For each year, the maximum life expectancy approximated the 5% trimmed mean life expectancy observed in countries with annual incomes greater than $12,276.
source: For each year, the maximum life expectancy approximated the 5% trimmed mean life expectancy observed in countries with annual incomes greater than $12,276 (t(8) = −1.596, p=0.149, not statistically significant; Table 1).
evidence: This is a validation result showing that the maximum life expectancy parameter is empirically grounded.

claim: Maximum life expectancy and critical income parameters were not sensitive to the random removal of 5% of the data.
source: In addition, we performed a sensitivity analysis on the maximum life expectancy and critical income parameters and determined that both were not sensitive to the random removal of 5% of the data (t(8) = 1.07, p=0.314, not statistically significant; t(8) = 1.46, p=0.178, not statistically significant, respectively; Table 1).
evidence: This is a sensitivity analysis result showing the robustness of the parameters.

claim: The maximal life expectancy rose from 67.8 years (95% uncertainty interval 65.4–70.1 years) in 1970 to 75.5 years (95% uncertainty interval 73.9–77.1 years) in 2007.
source: The maximal life expectancy rose from 67.8 years (95% uncertainty interval 65.4–70.1 years) in 1970 to 75.5 years (95% uncertainty interval 73.9–77.1 years) in 2007.
evidence: This is a result from the MM model analysis, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The change in maximal life expectancy represents a linear increase of 75 (95% uncertainty interval 48–99 years) days per calendar year (R2 = 0.875) over the last 40 years.
source: This change in maximal life expectancy represents a linear increase of 75 (95% uncertainty interval 48–99 years) days per calendar year (R2 = 0.875) over the last 40 years
evidence: This is a statistical result from the trend analysis of maximal life expectancy.

claim: The increase in maximal life expectancy of 75 days per calendar year is comparable to the life expectancy increase of almost 90 days per calendar year for the 20th century.
source: and is comparable to the life expectancy increase of almost 90 days per calendar year for the 20th century (Oeppen, 2002).
evidence: This comparison is made by the authors and supported by a citation to Oeppen (2002).

claim: The critical income needed to achieve half of maximal overall life expectancy declined from $1.48 ($1.18–$1.78) in 1970 to $1.21 ($0.98–$1.44) in 2007.
source: The critical income (in constant 2005 international dollars) needed to achieve half of maximal overall life expectancy declined from $1.48 ($1.18–$1.78) in 1970 to $1.21 ($0.98–$1.44) in 2007
evidence: This is a result from the MM model analysis, also shown in Table 1.

claim: The critical income in 2007 ($1.21) is equivalent to the extreme poverty line of $1.25 per day.
source: equivalent in 2007 to the extreme poverty line of $1.25 per day
evidence: This is a comparison made by the authors to contextualize the critical income value.

claim: The decline in critical income from 1970 to 2007 represents an 18% decrease in critical income to gain almost 4 additional years of life expectancy.
source: this represents an 18% decrease in critical income to gain almost 4 additional years of life expectancy.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the critical income and maximal life expectancy values.

claim: Critical income declined linearly at a rate of −$0.09 per decade (−$0.06 to −$0.13, R2 = 0.839).
source: Critical income declined linearly at a rate of −$0.09 per decade (−$0.06 to −$0.13, R2 = 0.839).
evidence: This is a statistical result from the trend analysis of critical income.

claim: Maximum survival for all age groups rose at statistically the same rate between 1970 and 2007.
source: Maximum survival for all age groups rose at statistically the same rate between 1970 and 2007 (Figure 3A, Table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by data in Figure 3A and Table 3.

claim: Maximum child survival to the age of 5 years increased from 94.5% (92.7–96.2%) to 98.0% (97.3–98.6%), an increase of 0.8% (0.3–1.3%) per decade (R2 = 0.665).
source: Maximum child survival to the age of 5 years increased from 94.5% (92.7–96.2%) to 98.0% (97.3–98.6%), an increase of 0.8% (0.3–1.3%) per decade (R2 = 0.665)
evidence: This is a result from the MM model analysis for child survival, also shown in Table 3.

claim: Maximum adult female survival at ages 15–59 years rose from 85.9% (84.1–87.7%) to 90.1% (87.8–92.3%), an increase of 1.1% (0.5–1.6%) per decade (R2 = 0.762).
source: maximum adult female survival at ages 15–59 years rose from 85.9% (84.1–87.7%) to 90.1% (87.8–92.3%), an increase of 1.1% (0.5–1.6%) per decade (R2 = 0.762)
evidence: This is a result from the MM model analysis for adult female survival, also shown in Table 3.

claim: Maximum adult male survival at ages 15–59 years rose from 77.7% (75.6–79.7%) to 82.1% (79.0–85.0%), an increase of 1.1% (0.6–1.7%) per decade (R2 = 0.749).
source: and maximum adult male survival at ages 15–59 years rose from 77.7% (75.6–79.7%) to 82.1% (79.0–85.0%), an increase of 1.1% (0.6–1.7%) per decade (R2 = 0.749).
evidence: This is a result from the MM model analysis for adult male survival, also shown in Table 3.

claim: From 1970 to 1980, the critical income values for children, adult males, and adult females were statistically equivalent, between $0.54–$0.58 per day.
source: From 1970 to 1980, the critical income values for children, adult males, and adult females were statistically equivalent, between $0.54–$0.58 per day.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be verified from Table 3.

claim: Over the 40-year period from 1970 to 2010, the critical income for child survival fell by over half from $0.58 ($0.46–$0.70) to $0.24 ($0.20–$0.28).
source: Over the 40-year period from 1970 to 2010, the critical income for child survival fell by over half from $0.58 ($0.46–$0.70) to $0.24 ($0.20–$0.28).
evidence: This is a result from the MM model analysis for child survival, also shown in Table 3.

claim: Critical income more than doubled for adult male survival from $0.54 ($0.38–$0.71) to $1.20 ($0.81–$1.58).
source: In contrast, critical income more than doubled for adult male survival from $0.54 ($0.38–$0.71) to $1.20 ($0.81–$1.58)
evidence: This is a result from the MM model analysis for adult male survival, also shown in Table 3.

claim: Critical income rose over 50% for adult female survival from $0.57 ($0.43–$0.70) to $0.89 ($0.65–$1.12).
source: and rose over 50% for adult female survival from $0.57 ($0.43–$0.70) to $0.89 ($0.65–$1.12)
evidence: This is a result from the MM model analysis for adult female survival, also shown in Table 3.

claim: The 1970 and 2007 survival curves for adult men crossed over at a value for $10.95 GDP per capita per day.
source: The 1970 and 2007 survival curves for adult men crossed over at a value for $10.95 GDP per capita per day.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: There are 58 countries with a total adult male population of approximately 780 million (or 35% of the world adult male population) below $10.95 GDP per capita per day.
source: There are 58 countries with a total adult male population of approximately 780 million (or 35% of the world adult male population) below this income value.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the income threshold and population data.

claim: For countries below $10.95 GDP per capita per day, adult male survival was lower in 2007 than in 1970.
source: For these countries, adult male survival was lower in 2007 than in 1970 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: For women, the 1970 and 2007 survival curves crossed at a value of $5.93 GDP per capita per day.
source: For women, the comparable 1970 and 2007 survival curves crossed at a value of $5.93 GDP per capita per day
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: There are 32 countries with approximately 150 million women (or 7% of the world adult female population) below $5.93 GDP per capita per day, where female survival in 2007 was worse than in 1970.
source: corresponding to 32 countries, with approximately 150 million women (or 7% of the world adult female population), where female survival in 2007 was worse than in 1970 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Between 1970 and 2007, for the 58 countries with an income under $10.95 per capita per day in 2007, child mortality improved by 11.8%.
source: By contrast, between 1970 and 2007, for the 58 countries with an income under $10.95 per capita per day in 2007, child mortality improved by 11.8%
evidence: This is a calculation based on the data for these specific countries.

claim: Between 1970 and 2007, for the 58 countries with an income under $10.95 per capita per day in 2007, adult male survival fell by 2.7%.
source: adult male survival fell by 2.7%
evidence: This is a calculation based on the data for these specific countries.

claim: Between 1970 and 2007, for the 58 countries with an income under $10.95 per capita per day in 2007, incomes rose by 8.9% (or an absolute increase of $0.98).
source: and incomes rose by 8.9% (or an absolute increase of $0.98).
evidence: This is a calculation based on the income data for these specific countries.

claim: For adult males in the year 2000, HIV prevalence (range 0.06–26% aged 15–49 years) and cigarette consumption (range 54.6–3385.2 per year at ages 15 years or older) were shown to influence critical income.
source: For adult males in the year 2000, HIV prevalence (range 0.06–26% aged 15–49 years) and cigarette consumption (range 54.6–3385.2 per year at ages 15 years or older) were shown to influence critical income.
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Figure 5 and Table 4.

claim: For the 86 countries with complete survival, income, HIV, and cigarette data in 2000, the critical income value was $2.02 ($1.32–$2.73).
source: Selecting the 86 countries with complete survival, income, HIV, and cigarette data, the critical income value was $2.02 ($1.32–$2.73).
evidence: This is a result from the analysis of the subset of countries with complete data.

claim: Adjusting for HIV and smoking prevalence to the average across countries reduced the critical income to $1.22 ($0.76–$1.69).
source: Adjusting for HIV and smoking prevalence to the average across countries reduced the critical income to $1.22 ($0.76–$1.69)
evidence: This is a result from the adjusted analysis shown in Figure 5.

claim: HIV and smoking could explain about half of the increases in critical income for adult males.
source: meaning that HIV and smoking could explain about half of the increases in critical income.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of adjusted and unadjusted critical income values.

claim: In 1970, the critical income for adult males was $0.54 ($0.38–$0.71).
source: In 1970, the critical income was $0.54 ($0.38–$0.71)
evidence: This is stated in the text and shown in Table 3.

claim: HIV infection and smoking do not explain all of the worsening of critical income observed by the year 2000 for adult males.
source: thus, HIV infection and smoking do not explain all of the worsening of critical income observed by the year 2000.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing the 1970 critical income with the adjusted 2000 critical income.

claim: HIV infection and smoking had no statistical impact on the maximum survival.
source: HIV infection and smoking had no statistical impact on the maximum survival.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a result of the analysis.

claim: Over the 10-year period from 1990 to 2000, a rise of one cigarette consumed per day per person led to a $1.70 ($0.96–$2.43) increase in critical income for adult men.
source: Over the 10-year period from 1990 to 2000, a rise of one cigarette consumed per day per person and 1% in HIV prevalence led, for adult men, to a $1.70 ($0.96–$2.43) and $0.70 ($0.27–$1.13) increase in critical income, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the first differences analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: Over the 10-year period from 1990 to 2000, a 1% rise in HIV prevalence led to a $0.70 ($0.27–$1.13) increase in critical income for adult men.
source: Over the 10-year period from 1990 to 2000, a rise of one cigarette consumed per day per person and 1% in HIV prevalence led, for adult men, to a $1.70 ($0.96–$2.43) and $0.70 ($0.27–$1.13) increase in critical income, respectively.
evidence: This is a result from the first differences analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: For adult females, the impact of a 1% rise in HIV prevalence per capita was associated with a $0.40 ($0.31–$0.49) increase in critical income.
source: For adult females, the impact of a 1% rise in HIV prevalence per capita was associated with a $0.40 ($0.31–$0.49) increase in critical income
evidence: This is a result from the first differences analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: For adult females, the impact of smoking was lower, with a change of $0.38 ($0.23–$0.54) per cigarette consumed per day per person.
source: however, the impact of smoking was lower, with a change of $0.38 ($0.23–$0.54).
evidence: This is a result from the first differences analysis shown in Table 4.

claim: Adding a covariate for HIV prevalence improved the goodness of fit dramatically for all years and genders.
source: Moreover, adding a covariate for HIV prevalence also improved the goodness of fit dramatically for all years and genders (Table 3).
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be verified from Table 3.

claim: Child survival replicates the upward and lateral trend in the original Preston curve for life expectancy.
source: Unlike for adults, child survival replicates the upward and lateral trend in the original Preston curve for life expectancy.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results showing declining critical income and rising maximum survival for children.

claim: For low- and middle-income countries, the majority of the past gains in life expectancy have been achieved via declining child mortality.
source: This suggests that for low- and middle-income countries, the majority of the past gains in life expectancy have been achieved via declining child mortality.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the child survival results and is consistent with UN data.

claim: The greatest decline in child critical income was achieved after 1990, coinciding with actions following the UN's World Summit for Children.
source: The greatest decline in child critical income was achieved after 1990, coinciding with actions following the UN's World Summit for Children.
evidence: This is stated in the text and can be verified from Table 3 and Figure 3B.

claim: Cost-effective interventions have been disproportionately devoted to child and maternal health.
source: With justification, cost-effective interventions have been disproportionately devoted to child and maternal health (Daar et al., 2007)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Daar et al. (2007).

claim: Increasing coverage of inexpensive health interventions such as immunization, insecticide-treated nets, and case management of childhood infections could be contributing to the decline in critical income for child survival.
source: Increasing coverage of inexpensive health interventions such as immunization, insecticide-treated nets, and case management of childhood infections could be contributing to the decline in critical income for child survival (Jamison et al., 2006; Mathers et al., 2008).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by citations to Jamison et al. (2006) and Mathers et al. (2008).

claim: There might be complementary benefits of education in reducing child mortality.
source: Moreover, there might be complementary benefits of education in reducing child mortality (Gakidou et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to Gakidou et al. (2010).

claim: The achievement of the UN MDG 4 (to reduce child mortality by two-thirds from 1990 levels) might be due to the falling levels of income needed to increase child survival.
source: Our study does not address any causal relationship between such interventions and reductions in child mortality; however, our results imply that the achievement of the UN MDG 4 (to reduce child mortality by two-thirds from 1990 levels) might be due to the falling levels of income needed to increase child survival.
evidence: This is an inference drawn by the authors from their results on declining critical income for children.

claim: For adult survival, there is a reversal of fortune compared to child survival.
source: For adult survival, however, there is a reversal of fortune.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the data showing rising critical income for adults.

claim: While achievable adult survival rates have improved, improvements are only associated with those countries at higher income levels.
source: While achievable adult survival rates have improved, improvements are only associated with those countries at higher income levels.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the results showing rising critical income for adults.

claim: The rise in critical income suggests that the marginal costs of increasing adult longevity are rising.
source: The rise in critical income suggests that the marginal costs of increasing adult longevity are rising
evidence: This is an inference drawn by the authors from the rising critical income for adults.

claim: The rise in critical income may explain the lower rate of decline in adult mortality in countries with low income.
source: this may explain the lower rate of decline in adult mortality in countries with low income (Rajaratnam et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to Rajaratnam et al. (2010).

claim: The emergence of HIV/AIDS in the 1980s and the rise in global smoking prevalence in low- and middle-income countries can explain much, but not the entire rise in critical income for adult males.
source: The emergence of HIV/AIDS in the 1980s and the rise in global smoking prevalence in low- and middle-income countries (Guindon and Boisclair, 2003) can explain much, but not the entire rise in critical income for adult males.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the analysis in Figure 5 and Table 4.

claim: For males, the rise in smoking accounts for over 40% more of the variance in critical income compared to 30% for HIV/AIDS.
source: For males, the rise in smoking accounts for over 40% more of the variance in critical income compared to 30% for HIV/AIDS.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the standardized coefficients in Table 4.

claim: For adult women, the impact of cigarettes on critical income is much lower, which reflects the five times lower prevalence of smoking among women compared to men.
source: For adult women, the impact of cigarettes on critical income is much lower, which reflects the five times lower prevalence of smoking among women compared to men (Guindon and Boisclair, 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by a citation to Guindon and Boisclair (2003).

claim: Even low levels (4%) of HIV prevalence in rural Tanzania can increase overall adult mortality by more than 50%.
source: Even low levels (4%) of HIV prevalence in rural Tanzania can increase overall adult mortality by more than 50% (Todd et al., 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Todd et al. (1997).

claim: Smoking increases critical income but has no statistical impact on maximum survival.
source: Our findings also show that smoking increases critical income but has no statistical impact on maximum survival.
evidence: This is stated in the text as a result of the analysis.

claim: Prevalence of smoking (and subsequently the deaths attributed to smoking) are rising in low- and middle-income countries but declining in high-income countries.
source: This is in line with trends in global smoking, where prevalence of smoking (and subsequently the deaths attributed to smoking) are rising in low- and middle-income countries but declining in high-income countries (Jha, 2009).

claim: An approximate national income per capita of $2.20 per day would be required in 2007 to attain the same achievable adult male survival rate with $1.25 per day in 1970.
source: Under the current conditions, an approximate national income per capita of $2.20 per day would be required in 2007 to attain the same achievable adult male survival rate with $1.25 per day in 1970.
evidence: This is a calculation based on the critical income values for adult males in 1970 and 2007.

claim: Should the critical income costs for adults continue to rise (in line with current trends), survival rates for low- and middle-income countries might well deteriorate into the future.
source: Moreover, should the critical income costs for adults continue to rise (in line with current trends), survival rates for low- and middle-income countries might well deteriorate into the future.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on extrapolating current trends.

claim: High-income countries have benefited from the rise in maximum survival among adults.
source: In contrast, high-income countries have benefited from the rise in maximum survival among adults.
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by the data showing rising maximum survival.

claim: The rise in maximum survival among adults in high-income countries is likely due to more widespread availability of secondary treatments for chronic diseases, most notably for vascular disease, and in particular from sharp reductions in smoking.
source: This is likely due to more widespread availability of secondary treatments for chronic diseases, most notably for vascular disease, and in particular from sharp reductions in smoking (Jha, 2009).
evidence: This is a speculative claim supported by a citation to Jha (2009).

claim: The probabilities of premature adult deaths before the age of 70 from vascular, respiratory, and neoplastic diseases are remarkably similar in low-, middle-, countries and high-income countries.
source: The probabilities of premature adult deaths before the age of 70 from vascular, respiratory, and neoplastic diseases are remarkably similar in low-, middle-, countries and high-income countries (Strong et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Strong et al. (2005).

claim: Low-cost, effective, and feasible interventions exist against chronic diseases, most importantly tobacco control.

claim: Low-cost drugs for secondary management of existing disease are effective interventions against chronic diseases.

source: However, these interventions are still not widely used in low-income countries (Jha et al., 2012).

claim: Over the past few decades, research and development of new technologies (drugs, vaccines, and policies) have focused mostly on childhood and infectious disease, with fewer worldwide investments for adult chronic diseases.

claim: The longer-term trajectory of critical incomes for adult survival might well depend on the development of newer interventions, as well as more widespread application of interventions already proven to be cost effective.

claim: This is the first application of enzyme kinetics to mortality changes.

claim: The MM equation has been adapted to the ability of organisms to acclimate to changes in environmental conditions.
